```{r setup, include=FALSE}
source("../setup.R")
docs_setup()
has_ragg <- requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)
has_av <- requireNamespace("av", quietly = TRUE)
```

Camera motion shows a fixed scene from several directions. Data animation changes the observations or geometry between states. This article renders both kinds of animation with `animate_3d()` and ends by opening the same plot in the interactive viewer. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html). Frames are drawn with [ragg](https://ragg.r-lib.org/), and MP4 output needs [av](https://docs.ropensci.org/av/).

1. **Build** the scene with `coord_3d()`.

2. **Move** the camera with `animate_3d()` and a camera path such as `orbit_3d()`.

3. **Interpolate** data states with `animate_3d(time = )` and `tween_3d()`.

4. **Explore** the plot with `view_3d()`.

## Example

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
```

The data describe a curved surface sampled on a regular grid. `frame = "azimuth"` reserves room for a full turn about the vertical axis, so the plot box keeps its size in every frame.

```{r static, fig.alt="A blue curved surface viewed at azimuth minus sixty degrees and elevation thirty degrees."}
d <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 12),
                 y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 12))
d$z <- with(d, exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / 2))
p <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "#2E6F9E") +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -60, elevation = 30, frame = "azimuth")
p
```

### Turning the camera

Without camera arguments, `animate_3d()` makes one full azimuth turn. The last frame stops one step short of the first, so the loop repeats no view. `format = "gif"` writes the movie to a temporary file; `file = "orbit.gif"` writes it to a path of your choice instead. Width and height are in pixels.

```{r orbit, eval = FALSE}
orbit <- animate_3d(p, frames = 24, fps = 8, format = "gif",
                    width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
orbit
```

```{r orbit-show, echo = FALSE, eval = has_ragg, fig.alt = "The blue surface turning a full circle about its vertical axis."}
docs_animation("orbit")
```

Printing the result in a document embeds the movie. Its path is in `orbit$file`.
The camera table contains one row per frame with its time and camera angles.

### Choosing an output format

The format chooses the file type; the backend chooses how the scene is drawn.
With a file path, its extension selects the format. Supplying a format alone
writes to a temporary path in the R session. When both are supplied, they must agree.

| Format | Result | Additional rendering or encoding package |
|---|---|---|
| `gif` | Animated image | ragg |
| `apng` | Animated PNG | ragg |
| `mp4`, `webm` | Video | ragg and av |
| `png` | Numbered image files | ragg |
| `svg` | Numbered SVG files | svglite |
| `pdf` | One page per frame | R's PDF device |
| `gltf`, `glb` | Animated model scene | See [Exporting plots and scenes](export.html#animated-gltf) |

For a few views that can be inspected page by page, write a multi-page PDF.
The vector backend retains vector geometry, with images for surface effects
that require them. Width and height are in pixels; dividing by dpi gives
the page dimensions in inches.

```{r pdf-views}
pages <- animate_3d(p, frames = 3, azimuth = c(-60, 0, 60),
  format = "pdf", backend = "vector", width = 600, height = 450,
  dpi = 100, progress = FALSE)
```

```{r pdf-views-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(file.exists(pages$file), file.info(pages$file)$size > 0)
```

For an image sequence, a file name such as `turn-%03d.svg` supplies the
frame-number pattern. With both file and format omitted, the return value
contains temporary PNG frame paths. Frames are drawn sequentially by default;
the `workers` argument controls parallel frame rendering.

### Camera arguments over time

Each camera argument accepts one value, one value per frame, or a function of time in seconds. Here the azimuth turns at 30 degrees per second for three seconds while the elevation rises from 15 to 50 degrees, one value per frame. A changing elevation needs room for every viewing direction, which `animate_3d()` reserves by framing the box as a sphere. `format = "mp4"` writes a video.

```{r rising, eval = FALSE}
rising <- animate_3d(p, frames = 36, fps = 12, format = "mp4",
  azimuth = function(t) -60 + 30 * t,
  elevation = seq(15, 50, length.out = 36),
  width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
rising
```

```{r rising-show, echo = FALSE, eval = has_ragg && has_av, fig.alt = "The blue surface turning a quarter circle while the camera rises from a low view to a view from above."}
docs_animation("rising")
```

Frames use the raster backend by default. `backend = "vector"` draws each frame with the exact vector scene backend described in [Visibility](visibility.html), at a higher cost per frame.

### Camera paths

A camera path describes a move as a timed sequence of views. `orbit_3d()` turns about the vertical axis, `dolly_zoom_3d()` changes the field of view while the camera moves along its line of sight, so the plane through the target keeps its size, and `c()` joins moves end to end. A field of view of 0 is the parallel projection, so the dolly zoom below flattens a perspective view into a parallel one.

```{r tour, eval = FALSE}
tour <- c(orbit_3d(degrees = 90, duration = 2, ease = "sine-in-out"),
          dolly_zoom_3d(fov = 0, duration = 2))
lens <- p + coord_3d(azimuth = -60, elevation = 30, frame = "azimuth",
                     projection = "perspective")
travel <- animate_3d(lens, path = tour, fps = 12, format = "gif",
                     width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
travel
```

```{r tour-show, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, eval = has_ragg, fig.alt = "The surface in perspective turning a quarter circle, then flattening into a parallel view at constant size."}
docs_animation("tour")
```

`camera_path_3d()` interpolates a list of keyframes, each a `camera_3d()` view, at the times given in `at`. Orientations are interpolated as rotations, so a path can pass straight over the top of the box without the spin that interpolating azimuth and elevation separately produces there. `fly_through_3d()` moves the eye along a spline through points in data coordinates.

```{r over-the-top}
over_the_top <- camera_path_3d(
  list(camera_3d(azimuth = -60, elevation = 30),
       camera_3d(azimuth = -60, elevation = 90),
       camera_3d(azimuth = 120, elevation = 30, roll = 180)),
  at = c(0, 1.5, 3), ease = "sine-in-out")
```

Passing `path = over_the_top` to `animate_3d()` renders it like the tour above.

### Tweening observations between states

The time argument names a column that holds the states. Layers without that column appear in every frame. The following example takes three cars from the built-in data and constructs a hypothetical second state with 10% lower weight and two more miles per gallon. Each car keeps its model name as its group, which pairs it with itself even though the second state's rows are in reverse order.

```{r point-states}
observed <- mtcars[c(1, 3, 8), c("wt", "hp", "mpg")]
observed$id <- rownames(observed)
observed$state <- 0
changed <- transform(observed[3:1, ], wt = wt * 0.9, mpg = mpg + 2, state = 1)
states <- rbind(observed, changed)
moving <- ggplot(states, aes(wt, hp, z = mpg, group = id, colour = id)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2E6F9E", "#9E5E0F", "#2A7A7A")) +
  coord_3d()
```

`tween_3d(n = 10)` inserts ten frames between the two supplied states. Statistics run on the supplied states before interpolation, and all states train one set of scales, so the axes stay fixed while the cars move.

```{r tween-points, eval = FALSE}
movement <- animate_3d(moving, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 10),
  fps = 8, format = "gif", width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
movement
```

```{r tween-points-show, echo = FALSE, eval = has_ragg, fig.alt = "Three cars moving from their observed weights and fuel consumption to lower weights and higher fuel consumption, against fixed axes."}
docs_animation("tween-points")
```

`movement$transition` lists, for every frame, the two states it lies between and the fraction of the way from one to the other. Group matching pairs occurrences within each persistent group, so map one identifier per moving mark when rows can change order. Source-row matching is also available, with row numbers counted within each state. Unmatched groups fade in or out by default; the `enter` and `exit` arguments of `tween_3d()` can keep them or set their starting and ending attributes.

### Motion trails

A trail counts preceding rendered frames, including the frames inserted by `tween_3d()`. Each moving mark leaves a tube whose alpha fades with age, and `taper = TRUE` also narrows the tube with age. Layers with fixed data appear in every frame, and a gap in an object's observations breaks its trail.

```{r motion-trails, eval = FALSE}
wake <- animate_3d(moving, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 10),
  trail = list(length = 6, radius = 0.05, taper = TRUE),
  fps = 8, format = "gif", width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
wake
```

```{r motion-trails-show, echo = FALSE, eval = has_ragg, fig.alt = "The three cars moving to their new positions, each followed by a tapered trail that fades behind it."}
docs_animation("motion-trails")
```

`trail = 4` uses a default tube radius of 0.5% of the diagonal of the panel ranges. Setting `width` in the list draws a ribbon instead, and `normal` sets its initial orientation. Radius and width are in transformed position units, and mapped `radius`, `width` and `twist` aesthetics also reach the sweep. `layers` selects the moving layers that leave trails. Trails follow the frame history of gganimate's [shadow_trail()](https://gganimate.com/reference/shadow_trail.html) and [shadow_wake()](https://gganimate.com/reference/shadow_wake.html), drawn as connected tubes and ribbons.

### Morphing a surface

A surface with the same grid in every state interpolates its heights and fill. The three states below hold the same sampled wave with signs $+1$, $-1$ and $+1$, so the movie returns to its first frame and loops without a jump. Halfway between two states every height averages to zero and the surface is flat.

```{r surface-states}
waves <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 10),
                     y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 10), state = 0:2)
waves$z <- with(waves, sin(pi * x) * cos(pi * y) * cos(pi * state))
wave <- ggplot(waves, aes(x, y, z = z, fill = z)) + geom_surface_3d() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2E6F9E", mid = "#E8E2C8", high = "#B5342B") +
  coord_3d()
```

```{r morph, eval = FALSE}
morph <- animate_3d(wave, time = "state", tween = tween_3d(n = 11),
  fps = 12, format = "gif", width = 600, height = 480, dpi = 100)
morph
```

```{r morph-show, echo = FALSE, eval = has_ragg, fig.alt = "A wave surface coloured by height that flattens, inverts and returns to its first shape."}
docs_animation("morph")
```

Positions interpolate in transformed scale units and colours in linear light. Paths with different vertex counts are resampled along their length, polygon rings are aligned before interpolation, and meshes whose connectivity changes cross-fade as whole shapes. [tween_3d()](../reference/tween_3d.html) lists the matching and transition options.

### Plots built for gganimate

The transitions of [gganimate](https://gganimate.com/reference/transition_time.html) run their own plot-building pipeline, and calling them on a plot with `coord_3d()` stops with a message pointing to `animate_3d()`. The same animation comes from the ordinary 3D plot: name its state column in `time` and add a `tween_3d()` specification, as above. Visibility is resolved again for every frame.

### Exploring the scene

`view_3d()` opens the same plot in the browser at its static camera. Drag to orbit, use the wheel or a two-finger pinch to zoom, and select **Camera code** to copy the `coord_3d()` call for the current view back into the plot code.

```{r widget, fig.alt = "An interactive view of the blue surface with orbit controls."}
view_3d(p, width = 560, height = 420)
```

[Interactive viewing](viewer.html) covers tooltips, selection, Shiny inputs, linked panels and crosstalk.

## Camera conventions

The camera path keeps the plot data fixed. [gganimate](https://gganimate.com/reference/transition_time.html) separates changes in data over time from its [fixed view](https://gganimate.com/reference/view_static.html); the fixed view informs the locked animation bounds here. [rayshader's movie renderer](https://www.rayshader.com/reference/render_movie.html) is the precedent for scalar and per-frame camera vectors and for encoders chosen by the file extension. [rgl's movie recorder](https://dmurdoch.github.io/rgl/reference/play3d.html) and [spin function](https://dmurdoch.github.io/rgl/reference/spin3d.html) supply the camera as a function of time. Rotation keyframes are interpolated as quaternions (Shoemake [1985](https://doi.org/10.1145/325165.325242)).
